2.1: Krishna sees Arjuna overcome with pity, eyes full of tears and despondent.
2.2: The first rebuke: where does this un-Aryan weakness come from, at such a moment?
2.3: Do not yield to impotence; shake off this petty faintheartedness and stand up.
2.4: Arjuna protests: how can I shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, who deserve worship?
2.5: Better to live on alms than to enjoy a kingdom stained with the blood of teachers.
2.6: Arjuna does not even know which outcome is better — to conquer or to be conquered.
2.7: The turning point: overwhelmed, he surrenders as a student and asks to be taught.
2.8: Arjuna can see no remedy for the grief drying up his senses, even in an unrivalled kingdom.
2.9: Having said 'I will not fight', Arjuna falls silent — the moment the teaching can begin.
2.10: Krishna, smiling, begins to speak to the despondent one between the two armies.
2.11: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet speak the language of the wise.
2.12: There was never a time when you or I or these kings did not exist, nor will we cease to be.
2.13: As the body passes through childhood, youth and age, so it passes to another body; the wise are not deluded.
2.14: Contacts with the world bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain — they come and go; endure them.
2.15: The one whom these do not disturb, steady in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.
2.16: The unreal has no being, the real never ceases to be — the seers of truth have seen the end of both.
2.17: Know that which pervades all this to be indestructible; no one can destroy the imperishable.
2.18: Bodies end; the embodied self is eternal and immeasurable — therefore fight.
2.19: Whoever thinks the self kills or is killed understands neither; it neither kills nor is killed.
2.20: The Self is never born and never dies; unborn, eternal, ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
2.21: Knowing it indestructible and unchanging, how can anyone kill or cause killing?
2.22: As one casts off worn clothes and puts on new, so the embodied casts off worn bodies.
2.23: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it.
2.24: The Self cannot be cut, burnt, wetted or dried — eternal, all-pervading, stable and everlasting.
2.25: The Self is called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable; knowing this, you should not grieve.
2.26: Even if you think it is constantly born and constantly dies, still you should not grieve.
2.27: For the born, death is certain; for the dead, birth is certain — do not mourn the inevitable.
2.28: Beings are unmanifest before birth and after death, manifest only in between; why lament?
2.29: Some see the self as a wonder, some speak of it as a wonder, and even hearing of it, none understand.
2.30: The dweller in every body is eternally indestructible; therefore grieve for no creature.
2.31: Considering your own duty, do not waver: for a warrior there is nothing higher than a righteous war.
2.32: Such a war, arriving unsought, is an open door to heaven for a fortunate warrior.
2.33: If you refuse this righteous fight, you abandon your duty and your honour, and incur sin.
2.34: People will speak of your disgrace forever, and for the honoured, dishonour is worse than death.
2.35: The great warriors will think you fled the battle out of fear, and you will lose their esteem.
2.36: Your enemies will scorn your ability with cruel words — what could be more painful?
2.37: Slain, you gain heaven; victorious, you enjoy the earth — so stand up, resolved to fight.
2.38: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike, fight — and you incur no sin.
2.39: This was the wisdom of Sankhya; now hear the wisdom of Yoga, by which you cast off the bondage of action.
2.40: In this path no effort is lost and no harm follows; even a little of it protects from great fear.
2.41: Here the resolute intellect is single-pointed; the irresolute have many-branched, endless thoughts.
2.42: The undiscerning delight in flowery words, saying there is nothing beyond ritual reward.
2.43: Full of desire, aiming at heaven, they prescribe rites for pleasure and power, leading to rebirth.
2.44: Those attached to enjoyment and power, their minds carried away, never attain the resolute intellect.
2.45: The Vedas deal with the three gunas; rise above them, free from duality, established in the Self.
2.46: To the enlightened, the Vedas are as useful as a well when there is a flood everywhere.
2.47: The most quoted verse: you have a right to action, never to its fruits — do not be attached to inaction either.
2.48: Perform action established in yoga, abandoning attachment, even-minded in success and failure — that evenness is yoga.
2.49: Action driven by desire for results is far inferior; take refuge in evenness of mind — the fruit-seekers are wretched.
2.50: One united in evenness casts off both good and evil here; therefore devote yourself to yoga — yoga is skill in action.
2.51: The wise, renouncing the fruit of action, are freed from the bondage of birth and reach the state beyond sorrow.
2.52: When your intellect crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, you become indifferent to what has been heard and is to be heard.
2.53: When your intellect, no longer swayed by scripture, stands unmoved in the Self, then you attain yoga.
2.54: Arjuna's question: what are the marks of one of steady wisdom? How does such a person speak, sit, walk?
2.55: When one abandons all desires of the mind and is content in the Self alone — that is steady wisdom.
2.56: Unshaken in sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger — a sage of steady mind.
2.57: Unattached everywhere, neither delighting in good nor recoiling from bad — such a one's wisdom is firm.
2.58: As a tortoise draws in its limbs, when one withdraws the senses from their objects, wisdom is steady.
2.59: Objects fall away for the abstinent, but the taste for them remains; even that ceases on seeing the Supreme.
2.60: The turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind even of a wise man who is striving.
2.61: Restraining them all, one should sit intent on Me; whose senses are mastered, his wisdom is steady.
2.62: Brooding on objects breeds attachment; attachment breeds desire; from desire comes anger — the chain begins.
2.63: From anger comes delusion, from delusion loss of memory, from that loss of reason, and one perishes.
2.64: But one who moves among objects with senses controlled, free of attraction and aversion, attains peace.
2.65: In that peace all sorrows end, and the intellect of the tranquil-minded soon becomes firmly established.
2.66: For the uncontrolled there is no intellect, no meditation, no peace — and without peace, how can there be happiness?
2.67: The mind that follows the wandering senses is carried away like a boat on water by the wind.
2.68: Therefore, whose senses are entirely restrained from their objects — his wisdom is steady.
2.69: What is night for all beings is waking for the disciplined; what beings are awake to is night for the sage.
2.70: As waters enter the ocean which remains unmoved though ever filled, so desires enter the peaceful one.
2.71: Abandoning all desires, free of longing, 'I' and 'mine' — that person attains peace.
2.72: This is the state of Brahman; attaining it one is not deluded, and even at the last hour reaches liberation.
